Kernel and image. For a linear transformation T from V to W between vector spaces, the kernel is the set of all inputs that map to zero. Ker of T equals the set of all v in V such that T of v equals zero. The image is the set of all possible outputs: im of T equals the set of all T of v as v varies over V. These two fundamental subspaces completely characterize the behavior of T, encapsulating its injectivity and surjectivity through their dimensions.

The kernel measures where T loses information. T is injective, or one-to-one, if and only if ker of T contains only the zero vector. The image is the set of all reachable outputs. T is surjective, or onto, if and only if im of T equals the entire codomain W. Both the kernel and image are subspaces. They are closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

The rank-nullity theorem is central to linear algebra. The dimension of ker T plus the dimension of im T equals the dimension of V. For a matrix, the kernel is the null space, consisting of solutions to A x equals zero. The image is the column space, the span of the matrix's columns. The kernel and image partition the geometric action of T. Some directions are sent to zero, while other directions contribute to the output.

Understanding kernel and image is essential for solving systems of linear equations and analyzing matrix rank. The first isomorphism theorem states that the quotient space V divided by ker of T is isomorphic to im of T. This connects quotient spaces to the structure of linear maps. Left and right inverses exist only under specific conditions related to the kernel and image. A left inverse exists only when the kernel is trivial. A right inverse exists only when the image is the full codomain. Understanding these conditions requires kernel-image analysis.
